mcqs.question: Which code shape reliably signals O(log n)?
options: A loop whose counter increases by a fixed step each iteration
A loop nested inside another loop over the same collection
A recursive function that calls itself twice per level
A loop that discards a constant fraction of the remaining range each iteration
mcqs.explanation: Logarithmic cost comes from repeatedly cutting the search space by a fraction — halving is the usual case, as in binary search. A fixed-step loop is linear no matter how large the step, since the step is a constant factor.

mcqs.question: A function loops once over n items, and inside that loop calls sorted() on the whole input. What is its complexity?
options: O(n² log n)
O(n log n)
O(n)
O(n²)
mcqs.explanation: The sort is O(n log n) and it runs once per iteration of an O(n) loop, so the costs multiply to O(n² log n). Reporting O(n) here is the classic hidden-sort error — a library call carries its own complexity into your loop.

mcqs.question: A problem states n ≤ 1,000,000. Which solution complexity is the interviewer most likely expecting?
options: O(2ⁿ) — exponential search over subsets
O(n log n) — sort or heap based
O(n²) — compare every pair
O(n³) — triple nested loop
mcqs.explanation: At n = 10⁶ a quadratic solution is roughly 10¹² operations — hours, not seconds — so the constraint is signalling n log n or better. Constraints are deliberate: they encode the intended complexity class, and reading them first tells you which approaches to skip.

mcqs.question: Why do most relational databases index with B-trees, an O(log n) structure, rather than hash tables at O(1)?
options: Hash tables cannot store more than a few million keys
B-tree lookups are actually faster than hash lookups per operation
Hash tables have a worse worst case, so they are never used in storage engines
log n is only about 30 comparisons at a billion rows, and the tree also supports ordered range scans that a hash cannot
mcqs.explanation: The logarithmic factor is tiny at real data sizes, so giving it up buys little, while the ordering a B-tree maintains enables range and prefix queries that hashing destroys. Hash indexes do exist and work fine for equality lookups — they simply lose the ordered access.

mcqs.question: A function makes two separate full passes over an array of n items, then one pass over a second array of m items. What is its complexity?
options: O(n + m)
O(n²  + m)
O(2n + m), which is a distinct class from O(n + m)
O(n · m)
mcqs.explanation: Two sequential passes add rather than multiply, and the constant 2 drops — but n and m are independent inputs, so collapsing them into a single variable would hide real information. Multiplication only appears when one loop is nested inside the other.
